haiku-low.q1: MySQL write and its outbox row commit together first. Postgres is applied after commit, with errors swallowed, so the caller sees success. The outbox row lets the drainer repair Postgres.
haiku-low.q2: Only when the incoming version is higher than the stored version (WHERE users.version < EXCLUDED.version), the id is not in the tombstone, and the copy holds pg_advisory_xact_lock(id).
haiku-low.q3: The step 4 gate must pass for 2 minutes: all running instances report users_dual_write=100, no deploy is in progress, and the oldest outbox row is under 1 minute old. Instances can disagree on flags for up to 30 s.
haiku-low.q4: One worker holds an advisory lock. It sleeps 10 s and rechecks whenever mysql_replica_lag_seconds exceeds 5, and reads the replica in batches of 2,000 rows.
haiku-low.q5: Reads need compare_last_clean_pass_at set. The source of truth moves after a 3-day soak at 100% reads, a clean compare pass under 24 h old, outbox age under 1 minute, an operator present, and standby and backups confirmed.
haiku-low.q6: The MySQL users_sync_outbox row, committed with the write. The drainer copies the current MySQL row to Postgres, then deletes the outbox row. Repair is retried until it succeeds.
haiku-low.q7: Every copy checks users_tombstone under the per-id advisory lock. Erased ids are recorded there and never reused, so a stale copy cannot recreate the user.
haiku-low.q8: Progress is in migration_state.backfill_last_id, committed in the same Postgres transaction as each batch. It stops when a batch has fewer than 2,000 rows, or when users_backfill is set to false after the current batch.
haiku-low.q9: The compare worker checks 10,000-id chunks by checksum against the replica, and also finds Postgres-only rows. After a 60 s recheck, persistent differences are counted and inserted into the MySQL outbox for repair or tombstoning.
haiku-low.q10: The MySQL fence closes first, and the Postgres fence opens before the flag switches to pg_primary, so at most one fence is open. If the deadline is missed before sub-step 5, the script reopens the MySQL fence.
haiku-low.q11: Postgres users_id_seq assigns new ids. At the switch it is set to GREATEST(MySQL AUTO_INCREMENT, max Postgres id) + 100000. On rollback, MySQL AUTO_INCREMENT is set to the sequence value + 100000.
haiku-low.q12: Writes go to Postgres and are mirrored to MySQL via users_mirror_outbox, with the mirror drainer and compare running. Rollback closes the Postgres fence, drains the mirror, sets AUTO_INCREMENT, reopens MySQL. The window ends at step 11, pg_only, after 14 days.

sonnet.q1: Order: open the MySQL transaction, take the shared fence lock, write, insert the outbox row, and commit. Then apply to Postgres after the commit, with a 250 ms timeout. If the Postgres part fails, the caller sees nothing. Errors are swallowed and the request succeeds. The outbox row stays and the drainer repairs it.
sonnet.q2: Only if the existing row's version is lower than the incoming version. The copy is INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE ... WHERE users.version < EXCLUDED.version. It must also not be in the tombstone, and the check and write run under pg_advisory_xact_lock(id).
sonnet.q3: The step 4 gate must have passed. users_dual_write is 100, and the number of instances reporting users_dual_write=100 equals the orchestrator's running instance count, for 2 consecutive minutes. No deploy is in progress, and the oldest outbox row is under 1 minute old. An operator then sets users_backfill=true. Instances can disagree for up to 30 s, because they cache flags and refresh every 30 s.
sonnet.q4: It reads from the MySQL replica, not the primary, in batches of 2000 ordered by id. If mysql_replica_lag_seconds is above 5, it sleeps 10 s and re-checks, because reporting jobs share the replica. A single worker runs under an advisory lock. Setting users_backfill=false stops it after the current batch.
sonnet.q5: To move reads, compare_last_clean_pass_at must be set, meaning one full compare pass found zero counted mismatches. Backfill must be done and the oldest outbox row under 1 minute old. To move the source of truth (step 9), the soak must have passed. Reads must have been at 100% for at least 3 days since T0, and the latest compare pass must be clean and under 24 h old. Outbox age must have stayed under 1 minute. An operator must be present, and the Postgres synchronous standby and tested backups must be confirmed.
sonnet.q6: The record is an outbox row (users_sync_outbox) holding the user id. It is kept in MySQL and written in the same transaction as the user write, so it commits with the write. The drainer, a permanent worker, reads the outbox, copies the current MySQL row to Postgres using the version rule, and deletes the outbox rows. If the row is gone from MySQL, it deletes the Postgres row and writes the tombstone.
sonnet.q7: Every copy (dual write, drainer, backfill, compare repair) checks that the id is not in users_tombstone. The check and the write run under pg_advisory_xact_lock(id). A delete writes the tombstone, and ids are never reused. So a stale copy cannot bring the user back. Backfill never copies a user already gone from MySQL, and the tombstone blocks stale replica rows.
sonnet.q8: Progress is kept in Postgres, in migration_state.backfill_last_id. It is updated in the same Postgres transaction as each batch's row copies, so the cursor is exact. If the transaction fails, both roll back. After a crash, the worker resumes after backfill_last_id. It stops when a batch has fewer than 2000 rows, and then sets backfill_done.
sonnet.q9: The compare worker finds them. It compares checksums of (id, email, name, plan, version) per 10,000-id chunk, replica against Postgres, and also finds Postgres rows gone from MySQL. For a differing chunk, it lists the differing ids, waits 60 s, and re-reads them from the MySQL primary. If they now match, it ignores them as a write in flight or replica lag. If they still differ, it counts a mismatch and inserts the id into the MySQL outbox. The drainer then repairs it, or deletes it and writes the tombstone if the row is gone from MySQL. A pass with any mismatch does not count as clean, and a new full pass starts.
sonnet.q10: The fences prevent it, not the flags. Step 9 closes the MySQL fence first, so every MySQL write on every instance returns 503. It drains the outbox, sets the sequence, and opens the Postgres fence. Only then does it set users_write_mode=pg_primary. An instance with a stale flag gets 503 and never writes to the wrong database. At most one fence is open at a time. If the switch runs long, a 30 s deadline applies to the script. Before sub-step 5 or on a missed deadline, it reopens the MySQL fence and nothing is lost. After sub-step 5, it uses the step 10 rollback. The hard limit on the write pause is 90 s, and the planned pause is about 45 s.
sonnet.q11: Postgres assigns them, through the sequence users_id_seq (nextval). At the switch it is set to GREATEST(MySQL AUTO_INCREMENT, max Postgres id) + 100000. On rollback, MySQL's AUTO_INCREMENT is set to the sequence's last value + 100000. The margin avoids reuse, and gaps are acceptable.
sonnet.q12: Every write goes to Postgres first, with a users_mirror_outbox row in the same transaction. It is then applied to MySQL inline (250 ms timeout) with the version rule. The mirror drainer and the compare worker (both directions) run continuously. Rollback is the switch_to_mysql script. It closes the Postgres fence and pauses compare. It drains the mirror outbox to zero and sets MySQL AUTO_INCREMENT to the sequence's last value + 100000. It opens the MySQL fence and sets users_write_mode=mysql_primary. The pause is about 45 s. The option ends at step 11 (pg_only), which is possible at least 14 days after T1. Once the mirror drainer is stopped, it is irreversible and a return to MySQL needs a rebuild.
